instantiated_cells.justification: The statute defines lobbying by reference to "any attempt to influence" specified governmental actions/decisions, without enumerating channels or modes of communication (oral, written, electronic, etc.).

"Lobbyist" includes every person or organization retained, employed, or designated by any client to engage in lobbying; "organization" expressly includes corporations, firms, partnerships, labor organizations, and public corporations, and §1-e(a)(1)(ii) specifically obligates public corporations to register, sweeping in professional lobbyists, in-house lobbyists, consultancies, law firms, and public entities; the statute does not separately enumerate think tanks or research institutions, and government employees acting in official duties are excluded.
The definitions section defines "public corporation," "public official," "state agency," and "municipal agency," but does not define the term "public entity."
The statute exempts from registration any lobbyist who does not expend, incur, or receive reportable compensation and expenses in excess of $5,000 (a monetary materiality threshold for coverage).
Lobbying includes attempts to influence the passage/defeat of legislation by either house of the state legislature and approval or disapproval of legislation by the governor.

Lobbying targets include the state legislature, governor, state agencies, and "public officials"; §1-c(l) defines "public official" broadly to include statewide elected officials, legislators, agency heads, officers/employees of state departments, and municipal officers and employees, covering legislative, executive, and administrative branches.
The definition of lobbying expressly covers attempts to influence legislation by either house of the legislature, gubernatorial approval/veto, and gubernatorial executive orders.
Lobbying expressly includes communications attempting to influence state legislators and the governor (legislative passage/defeat and gubernatorial action).
The lobbying definition encompasses attempts to influence both legislative action (either house of the legislature) and executive action by the governor.

"Public official" includes the governor, legislators, heads of state departments and their deputies/assistants, officers and employees of state agencies, legislative officers and employees, and municipal officers and employees — covering legislative, executive, senior officials, staff, and bureaucracy.

The definition of "lobbyist" expressly excludes any officer, director, trustee, employee, counsel, or agent of the state or any municipality/subdivision when discharging their official duties, so elected officials and public appointees are not required to register for official-capacity activity.

Public employees acting in official duties are categorically excluded from the "lobbyist" definition; the statute does not subject them to compensation, expenditure, or time-based thresholds as lobbyists (the $5,000 threshold in §1-e applies to lobbyists generally, not to public employees as a separate class).
The definitions of lobbyist, client, and lobbying turn on retention/employment/designation and attempts to influence governmental action — not on any public charter or special government protection.
The lobbying definitions do not turn on ownership; they turn on whether one is retained/employed/designated to engage in attempts to influence specified governmental actions.
The statutory definitions of lobbyist, client, and lobbying do not rely on the structure or composition of revenue of the regulated entity.
